explanation: The ADR focuses on adopting Lightweight Architectural Decision Records (LADRs) as a recommended practice for documenting decisions and rationale in the development process. It is about how the team works and documents architectural decisions rather than about creating or forbidding specific architectural elements or setting system properties. Therefore, it fits best into the Executive category, which governs development processes and organizational practices. It is not an Existence decision because it does not create or select system elements; not a Ban/Non-Existence decision because it does not forbid elements; and not a Property decision because it does not set system qualities or constraints.

The ADR decision is about adopting 'husky' as a tool to manage git hooks, which is a development process/tooling decision rather than about creating or forbidding architectural elements or setting system properties. The decision governs how the team manages git hooks in their development workflow, thus it fits the Executive category. It is not about an element of the running system, so Existence is not appropriate. It does not ban any element, nor does it set a system property or quality attribute.

The ADR focuses on standardizing the commit message format and integrating tooling (commitizen, commitlint, husky) to guide and enforce commit conventions. This decision governs the development process and developer workflow rather than defining or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. It does not create or ban any software element in the system, nor does it set a system quality or constraint. Therefore, it fits best as an Executive decision.

The ADR decision is about adopting a tool (standard-version) to manage versioning in the development process. It governs how versioning is handled during development and release, not about creating or forbidding architectural elements or setting system properties. Therefore, it fits best as an Executive decision related to development process methodology.

The ADR decision is about adopting TypeScript as the language for JavaScript projects, focusing on development process benefits such as type checking, IDE support, and documentation. It governs how the team works and the development environment rather than specifying architectural elements of the system to be built. Therefore, it fits best as an Executive decision. It is not about creating or banning a system element (Existence or Ban), nor about setting a system property or constraint (Property).

The ADR focuses on selecting and using a linting tool (TSLint) to enforce coding guidelines and automate code formatting during development. This decision governs the development process and tooling rather than defining or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. Therefore, it fits the Executive category, which pertains to decisions about development processes and tools. It is not an Existence decision because the tool is not part of the running system; it is used during development. It is not a Property decision because it does not set enduring system qualities or constraints, but rather enforces coding standards through tooling. It is not a Ban/Non-Existence decision as it does not forbid any element.

The ADR focuses on using a mock server as a software element to be included in the system setup to enable development and testing without relying on external API services. This is a decision about creating/selecting an architectural elements (mock server) that will exist in the system design to support development and testing. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general system properties, or dictating development processes, but about the existence of a specific element in the architecture.

The ADR focuses on enforcing consistency and style rules for CSS through linting tools and style guides, which sets enduring quality constraints on the system's CSS codebase rather than creating or banning specific elements or dictating development processes. This aligns with the Property category as it defines general quality rules and constraints.

The ADR decision is about adopting the practice of recording architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). This governs how the team works and documents decisions rather than specifying or forbidding any architectural element or system property. It is about the development process and methodology, fitting the Executive category. It is not about creating or banning system elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR primarily decides on the use of OpenShift as the container runtime and infrastructure abstraction layer, which is a specific architectural element to be included in the system design. This is a clear Existence decision because it selects a concrete software platform component that will exist in the architecture. Although the context mentions deployment processes and constraints, the core decision is about the inclusion of OpenShift as a system element, not about forbidding elements, setting properties, or governing development processes. Therefore, Ban/Non-Existence, Property, and Executive categories are less appropriate.

The ADR describes the decision to use Git as a replicated data store for deployment targets, representing deployment manifests in a hierarchical directory structure. This is a decision about creating and choosing a specific architectural element (Git repository structure and usage) that will exist in the system design to manage deployments. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general system properties, or governing development processes. Although it relates to deployment, it is about the system's architectural element for deployment management, thus fitting the Existence category.

The ADR selects ArgoCD as the deployment agent, which is a specific architectural element that will exist in the system to execute deployment information stored in git. This is a clear Existence decision because it chooses a component that becomes part of the running system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive). Although deployment tools can sometimes be Executive if used only in development, here ArgoCD is part of the deployment infrastructure, thus part of the system architecture.

The ADR decides to use Kustomize as a templating tool for Kubernetes deployments, which is a specific architectural element integrated into the system's deployment architecture. It directly affects how the system's configuration is structured and instantiated, thus creating or selecting a software element of the system. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general system properties, or governing development processes, so Ban/Non-Existence, Property, and Executive categories are less appropriate.

The ADR discusses various architectural options for implementing a Single Node Edge Server, including different configurations of nodes, operators, and container runtimes. The core subject is about which architectural elements (e.g., standalone RHEL with kubelet, custom operator, Podman, or OCP cluster) will exist in the system design. This aligns with the Existence category, as it involves selecting and creating architectural elements for the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR decision focuses on how to manage multiple demo instances by choosing among branching strategies, forks, or dedicated Git repositories. This is about organizing the development and deployment process and repository management rather than defining or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. Therefore, it governs the development process and environment setup, fitting the Executive category. It is not about creating or banning system elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR decides to introduce a new architectural element, a time series database, into the system design. This is a clear declaration that a new element will exist in the architecture to fulfill specific data persistence and querying needs. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes, but about creating/selecting a system component to be part of the running system.

The ADR describes the process and workflow for documenting architectural decisions within the development process, including how ADRs are created, approved, and managed. It governs how the team works rather than specifying any architectural element or system property. Therefore, it fits the Executive category, which relates to decisions about development processes and organizational practices. It is not about creating or banning architectural elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR focuses on controlling the cloning behavior of associations in the system by adding a flag to specific associations. This directly affects which architectural elements (associations) exist or are considered during the cloning process, thus it is about creating/selecting elements in the system design. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR sets a rule that certain API routes require a sales-channel-context-token to be provided, effectively establishing a constraint on how routes are accessed. It does not create or select a new architectural element (Existence), nor does it forbid an element (Ban/Non-Existence). It also does not govern development process or organizational aspects (Executive). Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision, defining a general enduring constraint on system behavior.

The ADR defines a general, enduring design rule about notification titles: they are pre-defined, globally managed, and standardized across the system. This is a cross-cutting concern affecting how notifications are presented consistently, which aligns with the Property category. It is not about creating or forbidding a specific architectural element (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR focuses on changing the development workflow for writing technical changelogs and upgrade information, including how developers create and manage changelog files and how the build process generates release notes. It governs the process and methodology of development rather than specifying or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. Therefore, it fits best into the Executive category. It is not about creating or banning system elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR defines the creation and use of a feature flag system as a structural element of the software design, specifying how feature flags are added, named, referenced, and removed. This directly relates to the existence of architectural elements (feature flags) in the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Although it involves some process aspects (e.g., deletion of flags after feature completion), the core decision is about the existence and management of feature flags as architectural elements.

The ADR focuses on refactoring document templates, which are architectural elements of the system's presentation layer. It decides on how templates are structured and extended, directly affecting the design and implementation of the system's rendering components. This is a clear Existence decision as it creates and modifies architectural elements (templates and blocks) that will exist in the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR describes the decision to integrate the app system, which is a software architectural element providing extension mechanisms, into the core platform. It defines structural and behavioral aspects of the app system, its extension points, limitations, and migration process. This is clearly about creating and selecting architectural elements that will exist in the system design and implementation, thus fitting the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system qualities or constraints (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR defines the creation and management of custom sorting elements for product listings within the system, including storage schema and mechanisms to add new sorting options. This is about introducing and managing architectural elements (sorting options) that will exist in the system, thus fitting the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR describes the creation and implementation of a new feature in the system: a customer group registration process for merchants. It specifies new data storage (foreign key for desired customer group), API route extensions, and admin interface changes to accept or decline registrations. This is about adding architectural elements and behaviors to the system, thus an Existence decision. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban), setting general system properties (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR defines how to encapsulate new features behind feature flags, including new entities, services, routes, and code changes that will be part of the system to be built. It focuses on controlling the existence and activation of architectural elements (entities, services, routes) in the system. This aligns with the Existence category, which covers decisions about creating or selecting architectural elements. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general properties or constraints (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR decision is about creating or selecting a specific architectural element in the system: a helper function to dynamically import ACL privileges from other modules. This directly affects the design elements (privileges and their mappings) within the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR decision is about creating a subscriber component that listens to a specific event and adds snippet translations for custom field labels. This is about introducing a new architectural element (the subscriber) and its behavior in the system to provide labels to the storefront. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes, but about adding a concrete element to the system design.

The ADR defines a general, enduring quality or constraint about how events in Shopware should be created and what context data they must contain. It sets rules on event structure and required interfaces, which are design rules rather than creating or banning specific elements or dictating development processes. Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision. It is not an Existence decision because it does not create or select specific architectural elements, but rather constrains their properties. It is not Executive since it does not govern development process or organizational aspects. It is not Ban/Non-Existence since it does not forbid elements.

The ADR defines new or improved architectural elements related to how the Data Access Layer (DAL) handles join filters for querying associations. It specifies the creation and behavior of 'join-groups' and how SQL JOINs are formed and managed in the system. This is about creating and selecting specific architectural elements (filters, join-groups) that become part of the system's design and implementation, thus fitting the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR introduces a new annotation '@LoginRequired' that is to be used in routing to enforce that certain API routes require a logged-in customer. This decision creates a new architectural element (an annotation) that affects the design and behavior of the system's routing and access control. It is about creating a software element that will exist in the system to enforce login requirements, thus fitting the Existence category. It is not about forbidding an element (Ban/Non-Existence), nor is it a general property or constraint of the system (Property), nor does it govern development process or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR decides on the architectural pattern for service decoration, specifically choosing to stop using interfaces and instead use abstract classes for service definitions. This directly affects the structural elements of the system (interfaces vs abstract classes) and how services are implemented and extended, which is a design element of the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), or about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Therefore, it fits best as an Existence decision.

The ADR describes a change in the API versioning strategy, specifically removing versioning from the URL and managing deprecations through minor and major versions. This sets a general, enduring quality or constraint on the API design and deprecation process rather than creating or banning a specific architectural element. It is not about introducing or forbidding an element (Existence or Ban), nor about development process or organizational aspects (Executive). Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision.

The ADR mandates a general rule about system behavior: always re-fetch data after saving to ensure data consistency and working with the latest data. It does not create or select a new architectural element (Existence), nor forbid an element (Ban/Non-Existence), nor govern development process or organizational aspects (Executive). Instead, it sets a design rule or quality constraint about data handling behavior, fitting the Property category.

The ADR defines a strategy for deprecations, focusing on rules, guidelines, and constraints for managing code changes, feature flags, and backward compatibility. It sets enduring policies and constraints on how the system evolves rather than declaring new architectural elements or forbidding elements. It does not govern the development process or organizational aspects directly, nor does it declare existence or ban of elements. Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision, stating general, enduring qualities or constraints of the system.

The ADR focuses on how nested line items in a shopping cart are processed by core and plugin cart processors. It defines the behavior and structure of processing elements (line items and processors) within the system, specifying how core processors handle flat line items and plugins handle nested ones. This is about creating and selecting architectural elements and their interactions in the system, which aligns with the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR defines rules and guidelines about when to use the Data Abstraction Layer (DAL) versus plain SQL in different application layers. It sets enduring constraints and policies on data access and modification to ensure extensibility, security, and integrity. It does not declare the existence or non-existence of architectural elements, nor does it govern development processes or organizational aspects. Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision, stating general rules and constraints about system behavior and design.

The ADR primarily sets rules and constraints on how ESLint is configured and used for linting the Vue administration app's JavaScript and Twig template files. It defines linting rules, exceptions, and custom processing to enforce code quality and style, which are enduring qualities and constraints of the system rather than decisions about existence or banning of elements, or about development process management. It is not about creating or selecting architectural elements (Existence), forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), or about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR decision is about introducing a testing tool (jest-fail-on-console) to improve the development process by making unit tests fail on console errors or warnings. This governs how tests are run and improves test expressiveness and developer feedback, which relates to the development process rather than the system's runtime architecture or its elements. It does not create or ban architectural elements, nor does it set a system property or quality. Therefore, it fits best as an Executive decision.

The ADR decision is about changing the placement and loading behavior of JavaScript scripts that are part of the storefront system. It involves moving script elements to the head with the defer attribute to improve loading and initialization timing. This directly affects the structural and behavioral elements of the system (scripts and their execution order), which are part of the running system to be built. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development process or organizational decisions. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR defines coding standards and rules for storefront controllers, page loaders, and operations, setting enduring guidelines and constraints on how the system should be structured and behave. It does not declare the existence or non-existence of architectural elements, nor does it dictate business-driven or process-related decisions. Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision, establishing design rules and quality constraints.

The ADR focuses on making 'shopware/platform' a stand-alone element for development and testing, effectively creating or selecting a specific architectural element of the system to be built. It involves structural changes such as moving development tooling into the platform, adding entrypoints, and adjusting scripts and environment configurations, all of which pertain to the existence and structure of software elements. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system qualities or constraints (Property), or governing development processes or organizational aspects (Executive). Although it touches on development convenience, the core decision is about the architectural element's existence and structure.

The ADR focuses on changing the build process architecture by adopting webpack-multi-compiler mode to isolate plugin builds from the core and other plugins. This decision creates a specific architectural element (the isolated build configurations) within the system to improve modularity and compatibility. It is about what is built (the build process and its components) rather than how the development process is managed, so it fits the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general properties or constraints (Property), or about development methodology or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR focuses on changing how URLs are generated in core mail templates, specifically making mail templates independent from storefront URLs by generating URLs inside the mail templates themselves. This is about defining the structure and elements (URLs) that will exist in the system's mail templates, which are part of the software elements to be built and run. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), or about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Therefore, it fits best into the Existence category.

The ADR describes the creation and definition of custom entities as architectural elements within the system, including their schema, database tables, API routes, and integration with the store API. This is clearly about creating and selecting specific architectural elements (custom entities) that will exist in the system design and implementation. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development processes or organizational decisions. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR defines a new mechanism for theme configuration inheritance, which introduces a new architectural element (the 'configInheritance' key and its dynamic behavior) that affects how themes are composed and interact. This is about creating and selecting specific design elements (theme config inheritance) that will exist in the system. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development process or organizational decisions. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR defines specific architectural elements for the payment system: two types of payment handlers (Synchronous and Asynchronous), their behaviors, and interactions within the payment flow. These handlers are concrete elements that will exist in the system design and implementation. The decision is about creating and standardizing these elements, not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category. It is not an Executive decision because it pertains to what is built (payment handlers), not how the team works. It is not a Property decision because it does not set a general quality or constraint, but defines concrete components. It is not a Ban/Non-Existence decision because it does not forbid any element.

The ADR defines new structural elements (entities and database tables) related to refund handling in the system, specifying how captures, refunds, and refund positions are represented and related. This is a decision about creating and introducing architectural elements (data structures and state machines) that will exist in the system design and implementation. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes, so it fits clearly into the Existence category.

The ADR describes the introduction of a scripting feature within the app system, specifically the use of Twig scripts that are saved in the database and mapped to scripting events. This clearly involves creating and integrating new architectural elements (scripts, scripting events, and their execution environment) into the system design. It is about what elements exist in the system to provide functionality, not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes. Therefore, it fits best into the Existence category. It is not an Executive decision because it pertains to runtime system elements, not development process or organizational concerns. It is not a Property decision because it does not set a general quality or constraint, but rather introduces new elements. It is not a Ban/Non-Existence decision because it does not forbid elements.

The ADR defines rules and guidelines about how data should be prepared and accessed for rule evaluation, focusing on enduring qualities and constraints of the system's data handling and indexing approach. It sets design rules and constraints on data retrieval and indexing to optimize performance and maintainability, rather than declaring the existence or non-existence of architectural elements or dictating development processes. Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision. It is not an Existence decision because it does not create or select specific architectural elements; it is not Ban/Non-Existence because it does not forbid elements; and it is not Executive because it does not govern development processes or organizational aspects.

The ADR introduces a new architectural element: a new 'increment' table and a new gateway with specific methods to handle increment/decrement operations, replacing the existing 'message_queue_stats' table and related services. This is a structural decision about what elements will exist in the system design and implementation. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban), setting general properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR decision is about merging multiple end-to-end (E2E) testing projects into a single project within the system's test architecture. This involves creating a new project structure and reorganizing test components, which are architectural elements of the system. Therefore, it is an Existence decision as it defines the existence and structure of software elements (test projects) in the system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational aspects (Executive).

The ADR decision is about adding the capability for plugins to include their own HTML file, which will be used as part of the system's administration interface. This is a decision about creating or selecting a software element (the HTML file as part of the plugin system) that will exist in the system design and implementation. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes, but about the existence of a new architectural element in the system.

The ADR describes the creation and use of architectural elements called 'component sections' and 'positionIDs' that allow extension developers to inject custom components and views into the administration UI. This is about defining and selecting elements that will exist in the system's design to support extensibility. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development processes or organizational decisions. Therefore, it fits best into the 'Existence (ontocrisis)' category.

The ADR decides to add feature flag support directly into the Storefront SCSS, which is a design element of the system's styling architecture. It introduces a new architectural element: a SCSS map representing feature flags and a function to query them within SCSS. This is about creating and selecting a specific architectural element (feature flag support in SCSS) that will exist in the system. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development process or organizational decisions. Therefore, it fits best into the Existence (ontocrisis) category.

The ADR decision is about adopting the practice of recording architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). This governs how the team works and documents decisions rather than specifying or forbidding any architectural element or setting a system property. It is about the development process and methodology, thus fitting the Executive category. It is not about creating or banning system elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR decides to install and use ACF PRO, a plugin that adds fields to the admin interface, as a component of the system's design. This is a decision about including a specific software element (ACF PRO) in the system, which fits the Existence category. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties, or governing development processes, so Ban/Non-Existence, Property, and Executive categories are less appropriate.

The ADR defines a naming convention rule for theme namespaces, which is a general, enduring constraint on the system's structure rather than the creation or banning of specific elements. It does not create or select a software element (Existence), nor forbid one (Ban/Non-Existence), nor govern development process or organization (Executive). Therefore, it fits best as a Property decision.

The ADR decision is about selecting a specific software element version (WordPress version tag 'v5') to be used in the system configuration. This is a decision about what element (version of WordPress) will exist in the system to be built and deployed. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development process or organizational matters. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR decision is about using a specific repository as the primary source for setup scripts and development environment files, consolidating maintenance and clarifying responsibilities. This decision governs the development process and organizational workflow rather than defining or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. It does not create or ban elements of the running system, nor does it set enduring system qualities. Therefore, it fits best as an Executive decision.

The ADR decision is about adding a package that enforces a constraint on package versions by preventing installation of known vulnerable versions. This sets a general, enduring quality or constraint on the system's dependencies, rather than creating a new architectural element or governing the development process. It is not about existence or banning of elements directly, but about a property (security constraint) of the system. It is not an executive decision since it does not govern the development process or organization.

The ADR decision is about running a validation command ('whippet deps validate') in the Continuous Integration (CI) process to catch errors early. This governs the development process and quality assurance workflow rather than specifying or forbidding architectural elements or system properties. Therefore, it fits the Executive category, which relates to development processes and organizational practices. It is not about creating or banning system elements (Existence or Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting system qualities or constraints (Property).

The ADR decision is about configuring the development process by using a dependabot.yml file to manage security alert rules. It governs how the team handles dependency security alerts and automates updates, which affects the development workflow and process rather than the system's architecture or runtime elements. It does not create or ban any architectural element, nor does it set a system property or quality attribute. Therefore, it fits best in the Executive category.

The ADR primarily decides on the technology stack for building an API, specifically selecting Python and the Flask framework along with certain extensions. This is a decision about which architectural elements (programming language, web framework, and supporting libraries) will exist in the system design and implementation. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general system properties, or dictating development processes. Although it mentions testing and deployment, the core decision is about the system's structural elements, thus fitting the Existence category.

The ADR decision is about sharing and using a specific architectural element: the Core DoS database by the Capacity Status API. It declares that the API will directly use and update the existing database, which is a structural decision about the system elements and their interactions. This fits the Existence category as it involves the existence and use of a particular system element (the shared database). It is not about forbidding an element (Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting a general property or quality constraint (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR primarily decides on the technology stack and framework (Django and related Python libraries) to be used for building the API. This is a decision about creating and selecting specific architectural elements (frameworks and components) that will exist in the system. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general properties or constraints, nor about development processes or organizational aspects. Although it mentions learning curve and developer focus, these are consequences rather than the core decision. Therefore, it fits best in the Existence category.

The ADR primarily decides on the authentication and authorisation mechanisms for the Capacity Status API, specifically selecting API Key authentication for a private beta and leveraging Core DoS for permissions. This decision is about selecting specific architectural elements (authentication and authorisation mechanisms) that will exist in the system design. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), setting general system properties or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Therefore, it fits best under Existence (ontocrisis).

The ADR primarily decides on the architectural elements and their interactions for the Capacity Status API, including the use of Django Rest Framework views, serializers, and domain models. It specifies the creation and structure of API endpoints, data serialization layers, and domain models, which are all architectural elements that will exist in the system. This fits the Existence category as it defines what elements will be part of the system design. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), nor is it primarily about setting general system qualities or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive).

The ADR focuses on how to implement a specific query mechanism (via SQL stored procedures or API module queries) to access user service permissions data within the system. This is about creating/selecting a software element (the query implementation) that will be part of the system's architecture to fulfill a functional requirement. It is not about forbidding elements, setting general system properties, or dictating development processes. Therefore, it fits best under Existence (ontocrisis). Executive is discarded because the decision is about what to build (query implementation), not how to work or develop. Property is discarded because it does not set a general quality or constraint. Ban/Non-Existence is discarded because it does not forbid any element.

The ADR titled '007 - FHIR Interface' is intended to document a decision about an architectural element, specifically an interface related to FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources). Although the details are marked as TODO, the core subject is about defining or introducing an architectural element (an interface) in the system. This aligns with the 'Existence' category, which covers decisions declaring that an element or artifact will exist in the design or implementation. There is no indication that the decision forbids an element (Ban/Non-Existence), sets a general property or constraint (Property), or governs the development process or organizational aspects (Executive). Therefore, the most appropriate classification is 'Existence (ontocrisis)' with high confidence.

The ADR primarily decides on the authentication and authorisation mechanisms to be implemented as part of the Capacity Status API system. It selects specific authentication methods (token-based authentication) and authorisation integration (leveraging Core DoS permissions) which are architectural elements that will exist in the system. This fits the Existence category as it defines elements that will be part of the running system. It is not about forbidding elements (Ban/Non-Existence), nor about setting general enduring qualities or constraints (Property), nor about development process or organizational decisions (Executive). Although there is some mention of process (re-evaluation in future phases), the core decision is about what architectural elements exist in the system for authentication and authorisation.

The ADR specifies a general, enduring quality constraint on the system: the proxy will throttle API requests to limit the rate of requests per second and bursts over a time period. This is a cross-cutting quality attribute (rate limiting) rather than declaring the existence or non-existence of an architectural element, or a process or organizational decision. It sets a rule about system behavior (throttling) to protect the service, fitting the Property category.
